After Marikana

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we take an indepth look at how Public order policing is still a massive challenge for police.

Unique Selling Point:
Widespread protest action and allegations of disproportionate use of force to quell demonstrations have kept the limelight on the police. Carte Blanche asks: Is the SAPS capable of dealing with a society in which often-violent civil unrest is an almost daily occurrence?

Summary:
On 16 August 2012, the South African Police Service opened fire on a crowd of striking mineworkers at Marikana. The fateful event left 34 mineworkers dead, 78 wounded and more than 250 people were arrested. And in 2015, the Farlam Commission recommended that a criminal investigation should be pursued against the police involved in the killings.

Over the last four years protest action has increased in South Africa, from service delivery protests to the University protests related to the increase of Higher Tuition fees, police have been called in to assist and in some instances this has led to violence breaking out between police and protesters.

In 2016, the SA Human Rights Commission made submissions to the UN Committee on Human Rights which in part highlighted “the high percentage of ... protests that turn violent, and the disproportionate use of force by the police to quell demonstrations.”

It would seem that almost four years after Marikana, Public Order Policing hasn't improved as police turn to rubber bullets and tear gas to quell protests.

Now almost four years to the day, Carte Blanche will track just what should have happened immediately after Marikana - in terms of effective police training.

The insert will thus explore how the South African police has improved or changed its training protocols not only in public order police but for other instances where police are called in.




Further information:
Interviews with the SA Human Rights Commission, the Centre for the Syudy of Violence and Reconciliation, a former Major General, involved in police training throughtout the continent and a Zandspruit Community member where police used excessive force to disperse protesters.

Press Release:


Policing the Protests

Widespread protest action and allegations of disproportionate use of force to quell demonstrations have kept the limelight on the police. Carte Blanche asks: Is the SAPS capable of dealing with a society in which often-violent civil unrest is an almost daily occurrence?




Script:


Script Visuals


VO: Yet another service delivery protest breaks out in the early hours of the morning.

Police move in, widely shooting rubber bullets and throwing teargas canisters towards tightly congested informal homes in Kliptown, Soweto.

A teargas canister lands in a yard just a few hundred metres from the chaos.
UPSOUND Slindile: TCR: 14:45:08:00
…. When they shot the teargas it went into the yard. When it entered the yard, the children were in the house, five of them and the teargas got them.

VO: Five young children are rushed out of the shack – their eyes burning as they cough and choke on the gas.

One of them, 4 month old Luyanda Hlwatshayo, foams at the mouth.

His mother Slindile is still shaken by what she saw.
UPSOUND Slindile: TCR: 14:47:28
I saw foam coming out of his mouth and he was coughing and that’s when I really began to panic.
LINK: CS gas or more commonly known as Tear gas is a dangerous chemical weapon that can cause severe eye and throat irritation – almost a burning sensation – it can cause difficulty in breathing and sometimes even vomiting.

It’s indiscriminate and affects everyone in its path – and for a four month baby old, the consequences can be devastating.

It’s traditionally being used worldwide as a weapon of choice to stop protests.
UPSOUND Chris Botha [0539:27] ...The moment it becomes violent, the principle of minimum force is the one that we start looking at – proportionality of force. So if it is necessary in terms of the threat to use then the specific equipment like tear gas or rubber bullets, and it fits into the process then that can happen.
VO: Chris Botha is a former Assistant Commissioner in the South African Police Service and a Professional Associate at the School of Public Leadership at the University of Stellenbosch. He specialises in police training.

UPSOUND Chris Botha [05:35:25]... in democracies all over the world – and in South Africa it’s not an exception – the principle of minimum force is accepted. It also means that if you have to use force eventually, it must be proportional to the threat that is used against the police.
LINK Before 1994, the police supported by the military, routinely used force to suppress political unrest. There were regular clashes with protesters and they were treated them with fear and distrust. But at the dawn of the new democracy, they were repositioned and under went a transformation to become a service to the people.
UPSOUND Commissioner Titus TCR 06:16:10:
… We had the experience under the Mandela era, Sydney Mufumandi era when his police really had to transform from the force to a service, from the Apartheid police to the Democratic Police Service…
VO: But the Head of the Prevention of Torture and Human Rights in Law Enforcement at the Human Rights Commission, Dr Danny Titus, believes this attitude of service changed with the rise in the country’s crime rate.
UPSOUND Comm Titus 06:16:10…
The intensity of the crime, the intensity of the violence, the organised nature of the crime as well, when we’ve realised that our peace dividend was really an opportunity for other people to organise against us in terms of security… then the call was very clear, we need more law and order, we need a stronger police.
VO: The police force underwent yet another transformation under Former national police commissioner Jackie Selebi. In 2004 specialised units such as the Sexual Offences, Family Violence and the Anti-corruption Units were disbanded and their highly trained members deployed to individual police stations.
UPSOUND Chris Botha [05:14:02] ... people wanted to ascertain whether we could bring more skills, competence, to the local station level, by disbanding the specialised units. [05:14:36] So in essence, the official reason was, if we take these people and their skills and competence down to station level, then we may be able to do more in terms of crime.
UPSOUND Lobo Das Neves: The disbanding of the specialists units in this country was a huge blow to policing.
You cannot expect a constable at every police station to know everything about every aspect of crime investigation. It’s just a matter of impossibility.
VO: With 25 years experience in policing, expert in international police training Lobo Das Neves says disbanding the units has had significantly negative consequences.
UPSOUND Lobo Das Neves We find more drugs available today than ever in the history of SA before. Organised crime is at its peak and police are struggling just to keep up with what is going on.

LINK: Things came to a head in 2009, as the fight against crime intensified and many criminals retaliated against officers, then National Police Commissioner Bheki Cele upped the anti and instructed his officers to ‘shoot to kill’.
VO: During a service delivery protest in Ficksburg in 2011, Andries Tatane became one of the most well known victims of police brutality when a video captured him falling down dead after being shot in the chest with rubber bullets fired by the police.

And then came the unforgettable day of the 16th of August 2012 in Marikana.
UPSOUND David Bruce TCR: 00:19:38:07
… the framework of the operation was disperse, disarm and arrest operation.
VO: Independent researcher David Bruce has done extensive investigations into the police’s actions at Marikana where police officers opened fire on striking mineworkers using live ammunition … Independent
Neves
Policing expert
UPSOUND David Bruce TCR: 00:19:38:07
.... the public order police do not have experience of disarming heavily armed crowds and the crowd at Marikana was heavily armed and so it was an operation that the public order police did not have the right kind of training or experience to carry out that kind of operation.…
UPSOUND Lobo Das Neves When you are in a situation like that when you see an aggressive group with firearms and other weapons and a shot goes off it takes a very special type of person not to open fire.
LINK TCR: 05:01:16:01
The killing of 34 miners at Marikana should have been a turning point for our police but according to a recent Human Rights Commission Submission to the UN, as more and more protests turn violence, our police are still using excessive force to quell demonstrations.

UPSOUND Comm Titus TCR: 08:23:36
They are using excessive force. That they are stepping outside the boundaries that the law allows. The police are entitled to use force; the police have the monopoly on force – but they have to do that within the bounds of the law ...

UPSOUND Chris Botha [05:35:25]... it’s acceptable to use minimum force steps when you need to deal with a threat. What becomes difficult is when you get to the possibility of using live ammunition that may cause the death of someone.
VO: And now four years since Marikana, police have had to deal with an upsurge in violent protests...
...from students protesting at Parliament and the Union Buildings in October last year during the fees must fall uprisings...

..to sporadic service delivery demonstrations throughout the country...

And often they also deal with protesters who fight back.
UPSOUND Enos Maake TCR: 17:22:43:19
Obviously people will fight back, you know they’ve got stones, they’ve got whatever they can throw at the police because they can’t just step there you know people shooting them, firing, throwing teargas inside our shacks.
UPSOUND Lobo Das Neves: I don’t know of any instances where a peaceful crowd was accosted by the police in this country and just shot at or dispensed chemical agents or rubber bullets or whatever the case may be. It’s a reactive form of police.
VO: In March this year, Enos Maake, a community leader from Zandspruit, organised a service delivery protest demanding electricity be supplied to the informal settlement.

But before long sporadic looting and fires broke out in the area. As police fired rubber bullets and teargas, protesters retaliated.
UPSOUND TCR: 17:18:29:06 Enos Maake: It escalated because we have public safety and that is down to the metro police and the police who knew about the situation in Zandspruit. They knew that Zandspruit is a violent society, they’re angry and then they didn’t do enough. We told them that we need enough police forces to be available; the visibility was not enough.
UPSOUND 02:46:10- Richard Mamabolo: ... under normal circumstances, peaceful protests, police are just there to guide and to make sure people do not get harmed.
VO: Richard Mamabolo is the Spokesperson for the Police and Prisons Civil Rights Union or POPCRU, one of the largest police unions in the country. He believes police often have no choice but to use strong force against protesters.
UPSOUND 02:46:10- Richard Mamabolo: .... in most cases that is a last resort really when protests are getting out of hand.... when protests are starting to take shape that seek to destruct property
LINK: But poor policing isn’t unique to South Africa.

In the United States for example, police are under fire for racial profiling and the persistent killing of unarmed black citizens. Sparking off a movement like the “Black lives Matter” movement.

So is poor training a universal problem and how do our police fair.
UPSOUND COMM Titus 06:16:10
I think they are very well trained. I think we have spent a large amount of resources in this country training our police.
UPSOUND 09:50:17- Richard:... post 1994 it has actually been changed to a 24 month period where as you would go for firearm training but also theoretical aspects of policing in itself, criminal law procedures for example and of cause public order policing as well
LINK: In many countries around the world being an officer is a calling, wearing the badge is regarded as an honor and it often runs in the family by in SA because of economic pressures, the situation seems a little different. People need jobs and as one National Commissioner put it, we often recruit the worst of the worst.
UPSOUND Lobo In some cases we are definitely recruiting the worst of the worst. Corruption within SA police at this point in comparison to other policing agencies, it is unacceptably high.
VO: New cadets undergo a strenuous training course, focussing on both physical and mental preparation for the job.

They are educated in Constitutional, Criminal and Criminal procedural law as well as the law of evidence.

They also undergo fitness and firearm training.
UPSOUND TCR: 00:17:20:05 David: The question of training isn’t necessarily the primary issue that comes out from Marikana...a big part... of what is often the problem with situations where police are using excessive force are questions to do with command, with leadership.
UPSOUND Chris Botha TCR 05:40:09.. I think one should also tell ourselves that training is not the panacea for all ills in the police situation a lot depends on the leadership on the ground....

PROMOS

One x 15 sec

Using Rubber bullets and teargas to control aggressive crowds, just how well trained are our police to deal with protests that turn violent.
UPSOUND: Training is not the panacea for all ills in police situations...
Two x 15 sec
The rise in violent protests has seen an upsurge in allegations of police brutality. Are police using excessive violence to quell demonstrations?
UPSOUND Comm Titus Police are entitled to use force but within the bounds of the law.
10 Second\In studio
Widespread protest action and allegations of the disproportionate use of force have kept the police in the limelight. Are they equipped to deal with violent protests.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): we take an indepth look at how Public order policing is still a massive challenge for police.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Widespread protest action and allegations of disproportionate use of force to quell demonstrations have kept the limelight on the police. Carte Blanche asks: Is the SAPS capable of dealing with a society in which often-violent civil unrest is an almost daily occurrence?
metadata.Summary: On 16 August 2012, the South African Police Service opened fire on a crowd of striking mineworkers at Marikana. The fateful event left 34 mineworkers dead, 78 wounded and more than 250 people were arrested. And in 2015, the Farlam Commission recommended that a criminal investigation should be pursued against the police involved in the killings. Over the last four years protest action has increased in South Africa, from service delivery protests to the University protests related to the increase of Higher Tuition fees, police have been called in to assist and in some instances this has led to violence breaking out between police and protesters. In 2016, the SA Human Rights Commission made submissions to the UN Committee on Human Rights which in part highlighted “the high percentage of ... protests that turn violent, and the disproportionate use of force by the police to quell demonstrations.” It would seem that almost four years after Marikana, Public Order Policing hasn't improved as police turn to rubber bullets and tear gas to quell protests. Now almost four years to the day, Carte Blanche will track just what should have happened immediately after Marikana - in terms of effective police training. The insert will thus explore how the South African police has improved or changed its training protocols not only in public order police but for other instances where police are called in.
metadata.Further information: Interviews with the SA Human Rights Commission, the Centre for the Syudy of Violence and Reconciliation, a former Major General, involved in police training throughtout the continent and a Zandspruit Community member where police used excessive force to disperse protesters.
